rubrics.criterion: For a record that already exists when a render-phase read or warm-up consults it, every settlement-state decision — that an error was captured and the read must rethrow it, that a response settled and the read returns it after refreshing expiry when a lifespan is configured, or that the record is still in flight and its promise is rethrown — is made inside the cache record structure that owns that state, not by the requesting code probing record fields (e.g. presence probes on error/response fields or timer juggling on the record) at the call site.
rubrics.rationale: This is the heart of the instance: the render/warm-up coordinator previously carried all four settlement meanings (error, response, in-flight, expiry refresh) as outside-in presence checks. A resolution relocates exactly those decisions.

rubrics.criterion: Creating a new record completes its lifecycle wiring where record state lives: the promise chain that stores the settled response and captures a rejected error, installation of the expiry timer when a lifespan is configured, and the record's removal/eviction callback are attached during construction (or an equivalent owner-level creation path), instead of being assigned onto the record's promise, timeout and removal fields by the requesting code after construction.
rubrics.rationale: In this instance the fresh record was a passive bag that only received keys and a comparator, with all wiring filled in from outside — the most legible evidence that record ownership was hollow.

rubrics.criterion: Deciding whether a record matches given keys — comparing the stored keys with the caller-configured comparator — is behavior owned by the record (or by the collection the record belongs to) and is not re-implemented by each cache-consulting call site.
rubrics.rationale: Key matching was spelled out three separate times over the same record fields in this case; unifying it behind the data owner is a distinct, gradeable outcome independent of the other moves.

rubrics.criterion: The collection of live records owns its membership: registering a record, finding the record for given keys, removing a record (found by record or by keys), and emptying the collection are behaviors of the collection structure, and no cache-boundary caller iterates, indexes or splices the live-entry array directly.
rubrics.rationale: All three centers in this instance reached into the same public array (indexOf/splice, linear scans) — the registry side of the envy relation, separable from the record side.

rubrics.criterion: Expiry refresh for a settled record with a configured lifespan (canceling any pending timer and re-arming it) lives inside the structure that owns the timer field, so requesting paths only trigger the refresh rather than performing it through the record's timer and removal fields.
rubrics.rationale: The timer dance was a distinct foreign field pair (timeout + remove) used by the coordinator; placing it in the entry is the cleanest single check that record-owned lifecycle truly moved, though other decompositions can satisfy R1 without it.

rubrics.criterion: Every cache-consulting path in the package — the render/warm-up lifecycle coordinator, the exported inspection helper, and the exported invalidation helper — is updated to route through the new owner-behavior surface, so no call path at the cache boundary still carries its own copy of matching, settlement probing, expiry handling or eviction.
rubrics.rationale: This case had three separate centers (a heavy one and two small ones at the entrypoint); relocating behavior while leaving even one center testing fields directly would re-introduce the relation at the next call site.

rubrics.criterion: The new owner-behavior surface stays internal to the package: the public export list and the signatures of the four public operations from the entrypoint are unchanged, with callers outside the package requiring no modification.
rubrics.rationale: The maintainer request fixes the public API explicitly; a resolution that leaks the internal restructuring into the public surface solves a different problem than the one asked.

rubrics.criterion: The reorganization does not merely relabel the same outside-in arrangement — e.g. the record stays a passive data holder whose fields are still shuttled in and out of it, or the old probing/matching code is renamed as a manager/service/worker module that keeps making the identical field decisions, with no decision actually owned by the data structures.
rubrics.rationale: Name-only moves are the characteristic hollow fix for this relation in this codebase's shape: the record class already exists to hold fields, so nothing but genuine relocation of decisions distinguishes a sound repair.

rubrics.criterion: Shared plain-data predicates used by the cache layer (the thenable test and shallow key-array equality with an optional comparator) are reused from one place by the owners, not duplicated as private copies inside each structure or call path.
rubrics.rationale: The extraction provided a leaf util module precisely so owners sharing matching behavior do not fork it; silent forking would be a small but real regression in the coordinated part of this instance.

rubrics.criterion: No duplicate declaration of the record's shape (a type alias or interface mirroring the record class's fields) is left coexisting alongside the class — the canonical shape of a cache record is declared in exactly one place after the reorganization.
rubrics.rationale: This instance carried a legacy record-shaped type alias beside the new class that described the same seven fields; keeping both is obsolete scaffolding from the split arrangement.

rubrics.criterion: No record fields survive that exist solely so outside code can wire the record up — e.g. a publicly writable removal callback or promise slot whose only writer is request-coordinating code — beyond the fields the structures genuinely use internally.
rubrics.rationale: The injected record exposed externally-assigned write-once fields (promise, remove) whose only purpose was outside-in wiring; a resolution that no longer needs them but keeps them invites exactly the old misuse back.

rubrics.criterion: The Suspense flow stays intact: while a record is in flight, a render-phase read hands the in-flight promise to React and settles on retry; once settled, the same read returns the response without suspending again; after a rejection, every subsequent read rethrows the captured error until the record is dropped.
rubrics.rationale: These three transitions are the library's whole reason to exist; the reorganization touches the exact code that implements them, so each transition is an independent instance-specific fact to confirm.

rubrics.criterion: Key semantics stay precise: a call without keys still keys on the function/promise identity itself, and a call with keys matches shallowly across the key arrays, with an optional caller-provided comparator receiving the corresponding key elements of the compared records.
rubrics.rationale: The identity-key behavior and the comparator plumbing both pass through the moved matching code in this instance; either breaking would silently change which records get reused.

rubrics.criterion: Lifespan semantics stay intact: reading a settled record with a configured lifespan refreshes its expiry, and once expired the record is no longer visible to inspection while a later read starts a fresh record instead of resurrecting the old one.
rubrics.rationale: Expiry was implemented through outside-in timer juggling over record fields here, so it is the behavior most at risk of drifting while its home moves; it must remain end-to-end correct.

rubrics.criterion: The non-rendering operations keep their exact effects: inspection stays inert (never throws, never starts a request, returns the settled value or undefined) and warm-up populates the record without suspending and returns nothing.
rubrics.rationale: Peek and preload read different corners of the relocated matching/settlement behavior in this instance; each corner must still be reachable with its original guarantees.

rubrics.criterion: Invalidation stays exact: dropping with no argument (or an empty key array) removes every record, and dropping with keys removes exactly the record matching those keys while all others survive untouched.
rubrics.rationale: Keyed removal previously inlined its own matching plus index arithmetic before splicing the collection; both halves of that path changed, so the observable removal contract is an independent fact to confirm.
